clue.text: Walked, maybe took bus 13 first

parts.note: the answer to 13 across is a thoroughfare, and its usual abbreviation is used
taking a bus is one way of travelling as a passenger, which is riding

explanation.surface: Someone walked somewhere, or perhaps caught the number 13 bus first.
explanation.walkthrough: '13' looks like a bus route number but is a cross-reference to 13 across, STREET, abbreviated to ST; 'first' places it ahead of RODE.
explanation.definitionFit: To have taken long purposeful steps is a particular way of having gone on foot, so the past tense is a synonym.

clue.text: Extra flash

definitions.meaning: first meaning: additional, as in a further helping or backup copy
a moment, as in 'I'll be there in a flash'

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a camera flashgun or a news bulletin; they are two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means additional as an adjective and a very brief moment of time as a noun.

clue.text: Warning sign that's self-evidently untrue?

parts.note: surface reading: a roadside notice alerting drivers to a hazard
setter's reading: the sign's two words, read as a sentence, claim the highway is functioning, when the whole point is that it is being dug up

explanation.walkthrough: The sign announcing repairs can be read as a subject and verb, a statement that the road is working, which is plainly false while it is closed.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the familiar notice placed where a carriageway is under repair, read whimsically as a false claim about its condition.

clue.text: Go north, entering remotest tangled place you might find anything?

parts.note: to go is to leave

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one piece goes within another
something tangled is twisted out of its neat order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Head north into the most remote, tangled spot, where you might find anything at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go north' looks like a direction to travel; 'Go' alone is the first piece, and the compass letter sits inside the jumbled adjective rather than reversing anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A large shop with many sections sells goods of every kind, so almost any item could be found there; the question mark flags the loose description.

clue.text: Golfer excited about a soft jumper will like this

indicators.note: about means around, so the other letters are wrapped round the added ones
excited things are stirred up and agitated, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
p (piano) is the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: A golfer gets excited about a soft sweater they will enjoy wearing.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper in the surface is a sweater, but in the definition it is someone who jumps. GOLFER is mixed up together with A and P.
explanation.definitionFit: The playground game involves vaulting over a crouching partner's back, so it would naturally appeal to someone fond of jumping.

clue.text: Dead ugly, oddly avoided getting uptight

indicators.note: avoiding the odd-numbered positions leaves only the even-numbered ones to be kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone extremely unattractive was strangely shunned and became tense about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead' here is the British slang intensifier meaning very, so 'dead ugly' reads as 'very ugly'; it is in fact just the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a nervous, tense, on-edge state of mind, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Party make Lancaster cardinal?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to celebrate wildly, going out on the spree
second meaning, read literally: colour a particular English town scarlet, cardinal being a deep red

explanation.surface: A political party wants to promote someone from Lancaster to cardinal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks like a noun and 'cardinal' like a churchman. Lancaster is a town in north-west England whose emblem is the red rose; the question mark marks the literal, whimsical reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means go out for a riotous night of celebration, which is what partying as a verb describes.

clue.text: Haul up wreck in sound

indicators.note: in sound means as heard by the ear, so spelling gives way to pronunciation

parts.note: to raze a building is to demolish or wreck it completely

explanation.surface: Salvagers lift a shipwreck lying in a stretch of sea water.
explanation.walkthrough: A sound is also an inlet of the sea, which suits a wreck being hauled up; here it signals pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: To lift something upward, such as a sunken vessel from the seabed, is a straightforward synonym for hauling it up.

clue.text: What gives info on psyche, ultimately, and personal quirks

definitions.text: What gives info on psyche, ultimately, and personal quirks

parts.note: gen is British informal for information

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of this word
tics are involuntary habitual twitches or mannerisms

explanation.surface: Some science reveals information about the mind and about one's individual peculiarities.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: 'on' means placed next to, and 'and' simply adds the last piece. Gen is everyday British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: The study of heredity explains inherited traits, which arguably include temperament and individual mannerisms, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Holds group studying drawing in Portugal

indicators.note: to draw something in is to pull it inside, so one piece takes another within itself

parts.note: a set of students taught together
P is the international vehicle code for Portugal

explanation.surface: A group studying art is taking a drawing course in Portugal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' looks like art lessons for the class in Portugal, but it means pulling in, the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To grip something tightly in the hand or arms is to hold it, so the verbs are synonyms in the same tense.

clue.text: Design it? I only should cover lighting

indicators.note: to cover is to conceal beneath, so the words lie over the answer and keep it out of sight

parts.note: the letters run on across the word breaks from the end of the first word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: A lighting designer is told they need only handle the illumination plan.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and the odd syntax break the run of letters across four words; ignore punctuation and spaces.
explanation.definitionFit: The act of setting something alight is a synonym for lighting it, as with lighting a fire or a gas burner.

clue.text: Change pounds, holding German one over

indicators.note: to hold is to grip, so one piece is clasped inside another

parts.note: a pound is an enclosure for animals, as is a pen

indicators.note: to turn over is to flip end to end, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: ein is the German word for one

explanation.surface: A traveller exchanges sterling, keeping one German coin back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pounds' and 'Change' both look like money, but pounds here are animal enclosures.
explanation.definitionFit: Small coins carried loose in a pocket are what people mean by loose change, so the plural coin name fits the noun.

clue.text: Report dividing partners — we rejected spin

indicators.note: to divide a pair is to come between them, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: North and South are partners at the bridge table

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round
to reel is to whirl or spin round

explanation.surface: A news story about a couple splitting up says we refused to put a spin on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report dividing partners' reads as a story about a separation, but 'Report' is the definition; North and South are a bridge partnership, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A short film of current events shown in cinemas was a form of news report, so the noun is a specific example.

clue.text: Way south lies beside bay, perhaps, west of Teignmouth

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation
the bay laurel is an example of this kind of plant, hence 'perhaps'

indicators.note: the western end of an across word is its left-hand edge, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of this place name

explanation.surface: A road heads south past a bay, somewhere to the west of the Devon resort Teignmouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bay' looks like a coastal inlet near Teignmouth, a seaside town in Devon, but it is the laurel; '…perhaps' marks it as one example of a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A public road in a town is a thoroughfare, and way is a common name for one, as in Abbey Way.

clue.text: Something written on little being seen in show

parts.note: a sheet of paper is what you write on
a tiny creature

explanation.surface: A note scribbled on a small child is spotted during a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little being' sounds like a child but means a tiny creature.
explanation.definitionFit: An elaborate public display or procession, often historical, is a kind of spectacle or performance, so the nouns match.

clue.text: One offers prayers to monarchical bust

indicators.note: something bust is broken apart, so its letters are smashed and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A worshipper says prayers before a sculpted bust of a king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a statue of a monarch's head and shoulders; it is the anagram signal, and 'to' belongs in the fodder rather than linking.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Western church headed by the Pope is a believer who prays, so the clue gives a loose description by example.

clue.text: Lover dressed up in denim, alas

indicators.note: dressing something up gives it a new look, so its letters appear in a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A romeo got dressed up in jeans, sadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like part of the fashion picture but only joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A womaniser who enjoys romancing many partners is a lover in the casual sense, so the phrase fits the noun.

clue.text: Winning upset half-hearted crowd

indicators.note: a heart with only half its strength has lost part of its middle, so one central letter is dropped

parts.note: an upset is a fuss or commotion
a disorderly mob

explanation.surface: A surprise victory disheartens a sullen crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winning' and 'upset' suggest a sporting shock, but 'Winning' means charming. The middle of RABBLE is a pair of Bs, and removing one halves it.
explanation.definitionFit: A winning smile is a charming, delightful one, so the adjective means lovable, the same sense.

clue.text: Just find underground in Paris is speedier at heart

parts.note: to disinter is to dig up from the earth, finding what was buried
est is French for is

indicators.note: the heart of something is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of this word

explanation.surface: Locating the Paris Métro proves quicker in the city centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like a filler word meaning simply, and 'underground' like the Métro; it means fair, and the phrase is a verb for digging up.
explanation.definitionFit: Being impartial and unbiased, free of personal stake, is what makes a judge fair, so the adjective matches the sense of just.

clue.text: Skills overseen by 13 institutes

parts.note: the answer to 13 across is a thoroughfare, and its usual abbreviation is used
arts are crafts or skills

explanation.surface: Skills are supervised by a set of thirteen colleges.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer one piece is 'overseen by' another when that other sits above it. 'Institutes' looks like a noun meaning colleges but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To institute something is to set it up or begin it, so the third-person verb means the same as begins.

clue.text: What's cooking? It's about done

parts.note: re means concerning or about
something done and finished is past

explanation.surface: Someone asks what's in the oven and is told it's nearly ready.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About done' reads as nearly finished; the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A meal is what is being prepared when food is cooking, so the formal word for one answers the question loosely.

clue.text: Scheme one's involved in leads to trial

indicators.note: something involved in a matter is caught up inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: a scheme or conspiracy
I is the Roman numeral one; the 's means is

explanation.surface: A conspiracy someone is mixed up in ends with them in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trial' suggests a court case for the plotter, but it means a test run.
explanation.definitionFit: A test run of a scheme or broadcast before full launch is a trial, so pilot works as the same noun.

clue.text: Under the softest cover, short nap must be disturbed by now

indicators.note: to be disturbed by an intruder is to have it break in, so one piece pushes inside another
something cut short has lost its end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: an afternoon sleep
taken as written

explanation.surface: Snug beneath the softest duvet, a short doze is bound to be interrupted right now.
explanation.walkthrough: The softest cover sounds like bedding, but it is a layer of fallen snow; SIEST is split after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground blanketed most heavily in snow lies beneath a soft white layer, so the superlative is described cryptically.

clue.text: Short measure's imbibed when tight

indicators.note: imbibed means drunk down, so one piece is swallowed inside another

parts.note: ft is the abbreviation for foot, a measure of length
as can mean while or when

explanation.surface: A small tot of spirits is downed when someone is drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short measure' and 'tight' paint a picture of drinking, tight being slang for drunk; here tight means firmly fixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Held fast means held securely, and a knot pulled tight is fixed firmly, so the adjectives share that sense.

clue.text: Revolutionary space scientists work in right place in Scotland

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the letters go back to front

parts.note: a laboratory, where scientists work
morally right, ethical

explanation.surface: Pioneering space scientists are working at a suitable site in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary space scientists' reads as groundbreaking astronomers, but 'space' is just a room. Balmoral is the royal family's castle estate in Aberdeenshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The royal castle and estate in Aberdeenshire is a well-known Scottish location, so the definition names it by its country.

clue.text: Diverted metro runs in quake …

indicators.note: in places one item inside the other before the letters are rearranged
a diverted route has been rerouted, so the letters take a different order

parts.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: An underground railway is rerouted as services keep running through an earthquake.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis leads into the next clue, continuing the earthquake story; it plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A small shaking of the ground is a minor earthquake, so the nouns are synonyms for seismic movement.

clue.text: … epicentre at Yerevan — location for appeal?

indicators.note: the words are the place where the answer is situated, so it sits inside them

parts.note: the letters run from inside the first word, across the second, into the start of the third

explanation.surface: Continuing the quake story: the epicentre was at Yerevan, the Armenian capital, so that is where aid should be sent.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to the previous clue; 'epicentre' looks like part of the quake news but is just fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An earnest request or plea is an appeal, so the two nouns are direct synonyms.

clue.text: A teacher is strung along in 'Dandy'

parts.note: taken as written
a don is a university teacher
taken as written

explanation.surface: A teacher is strung along in the Dandy, a long-running British children's comic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strung along' only means the pieces are placed one after another, not deceived. The quotes make Dandy look like the comic's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A beautiful young man, named after the Greek youth loved by Aphrodite, can be a vain, fashion-conscious fellow, close to the sense of fop.
